# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why4: The wearer appears twice, once as 'has the problem' and once as 'decides to buy', so two rows overlap where one row should carry both tags.
screens.why5: It still says what I typed: nobody else has to agree, and the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult is both the one with the problem and the buyer.
screens.why7: Nobody else is first and no role is invented, so the belief 'nobody else' matches my answer, but the card says the person with the problem and the decider share one row when they are the same person, and here they are split into two.
screens.instead: The people involved: Nobody else · Deaf or hard-of-hearing adult (has the problem, decides to buy). Add up to two who have to agree, 4 words each.

screens.why1: Right after I said nobody else has to agree, Keel confirms the one statement it will test before moving on, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: The title and belief are plain, but the bar's "paid for something for this" is clumsy and needs a second read; "paid for something like this" is what I'd say.
screens.why3: I know my wearers buy their own glasses, often with HSA/FSA money, so confirming that they decide alone is squarely what I know.
screens.why4: There is one row, Nobody else, my own pick, with nothing to choose between, and the escape back to name a role is offered plainly.
screens.why5: It still says what I typed: the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree.
screens.why7: A list holding only Nobody else is shown as a statement to confirm, and the belief reads nobody else rather than an invented role. Only decided alone counts for it, and the other three answers count against, so the belief can be refuted; the bar sits at 2 in 3.
screens.instead: Holds if at least 2 in 3 deaf and hard-of-hearing adults say they decided on their own the last time they paid for something like this.

screens.why1: After who decides, the cost, the price and who has to agree, the natural next question is what first step I'd ask a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult to take, and it comes before Keel drafts the stranger's item on the next screen.
screens.why2: 'First real step' is plain, but 'where any money goes' takes a second read, and the hint's examples ('pay for a pilot', 'let us run a trial') are B2B words that don't fit selling glasses to individual wearers.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I want a new wearer to do first: order the glasses on the 15-day risk-free return, which I run myself.
screens.why4: A free box with the card's allowed 'I'm not sure' chip fits a founder step that is one step; nothing is missing or overlapping.
screens.why5: The screen takes my words as typed ('order the caption glasses with free returns') and adds nothing of its own to them.
screens.why7: The box asks for exactly the card's founder step: one step in base form to follow 'would', at most 9 words, where the money goes. It promises the smaller free step only when the step costs money, data or a signature. My 7-word answer keeps 'free returns' and 'caption glasses', the terms that define it.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take, and what would it cost them? (one step, up to 9 words, e.g. "order a pair with free returns" or "try the free captions app")

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first real step, this is where I check how strangers will hear it and what Keel will test, so it obviously belongs here.
screens.why2: The four answers read plainly to my wearers, but the smaller-step line shows the garbled 'Yes, after Try a working pair of caption glasses first' instead of a clean noun phrase, so I had to read it twice to see what Keel drafted.
screens.why3: Whether they would order glasses for themselves is a decision my deaf and hard-of-hearing wearers make and pay for on their own, so they can answer it from their own life.
screens.why4: The set is complete and runs firm yes, soft yes, soft no, no, but 'trying a working pair first' overlaps with ordering under free returns, which already is trying a pair, so the soft yes is not clearly a different act.
screens.why5: 'Order the caption glasses with free returns' keeps my step and its defining term, free returns, and the belief adds no 'now', number or timing I did not write.
screens.why7: Ordering costs $599, so a smaller step is rightly drafted and the first yes names the step whole with two for and two against and no escape, but the soft yes ('trying a working pair first') is close to the step itself because free returns already is the trial, which bends the rule that the second answer must not be the step again.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you order the caption glasses with free returns, or not? Yes, I'd order the caption glasses with free returns · Probably, after seeing a live demo first · Probably not · No

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, after I've named my commitment step (order the caption glasses with free returns), asking whether to invite people to try it for real is the obvious last call.
screens.why2: Short and plain, and the hint spells out exactly what respondents will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want emails from deaf and hard-of-hearing people willing to try a pair is entirely my own decision as the founder.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for this choice, and no escape is needed for a founder's own setting.
screens.why5: The hint's line 'Would you try this for real?' stays generic and doesn't show my commitment step (order the caption glasses with free returns), so I can't confirm the ask respondents see still carries the free-returns order I typed.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you order the caption glasses with free returns? Leave your email." Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out, after the pilot offer, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but the choice is offered only as a 5-second audio clip; a deaf or hard-of-hearing founder like my co-founder cannot judge it by ear, and the hint says 'voice' while what I locked was the face.
screens.why3: I can pick, but for my people what matters is a face that is easy to lipread and clear captions, not how a voice sounds, so I would partly be guessing between Daphne and Saskia.
screens.why4: Two interviewers are distinct, but there is no visual or caption preview of each, and no option for a text-only or captions-first interviewer, which is the true answer for many deaf respondents.
screens.why5: The screen keeps my actor 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' and leaks nothing of AirCaps or the glasses to the respondent.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Show each interviewer's face speaking with captions on (Daphne / Saskia / text only, no video), so I can see which is easiest to lipread and read.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks, choosing how my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: The labels and descriptions are plain, and 'Read and tap' says exactly what my people would do.
screens.why3: I know my wearers read captions all day and many can't rely on audio, so I can pick the format from what I know of them.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and complete, and Daphne's line says every question is also on screen, so even the voice option doesn't shut out a deaf respondent.
screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps leaks into the format choice, and my pick, Read and tap, is shown as I made it.

screens.why1: Once the study is set to send, choosing who receives the links is the obvious last step, and nothing before this screen asked it.
screens.why2: Each option says plainly what I would do (send named links, pick a Keel contacts list, or post one open link with Google sign-in), so I can answer on the first read.
screens.why3: I know which deaf and hard-of-hearing people I can reach by name, from our users and the community, and which groups I could post in, so this is my own call.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach people, but there is no option for mixing named people with a group post, which is what I would really do for this community, and the second option leans on a Contacts page I may not have seen yet.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my study or shows my product to respondents; it only concerns how links go out.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? (pick any) -- People I know by name, each with their own link / A list I found with Keel's contact search / One open link I post in a group where they already are (sign in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside its deciding number (Existing sacrifice: 1 of 7 lose 12 or more conversations a month), though I'd have expected Price at 0 of 7 to be the card named as the worst.
screens.why_b2: Each card plainly shows what is counted, over 7 people, against a bar of 5 of 7; only the card numbering jumping from 4 to 6 and the tally printed twice make me look again.
screens.why_b3: Price, Buyer and payer and Commitment read as I typed them, but my cost estimate was $200 to $1,500 a year and Existing sacrifice now reads as 'about 12 conversations a month', which I recognise but never wrote.
screens.why_b4: The lines say what failed ('they value it below your price', 'they lose less today than you estimated'), but nothing says what to do about $599 when 0 of 7 reach it, and the statement under the verdict explains the interview, not the next step.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and nothing is called strong, but 'they lose less today than you estimated' speaks for all deaf and hard-of-hearing adults from 7 people, the small n is never flagged, and 6 of 7 'would order' is shown as holding beside 0 of 7 at my price without saying the two pull against each other.
screens.instead: Not holding up: none of 7 would pay $599 up front or $20 a month and only 1 of 7 loses 12 conversations a month, so test a lower price or a rental before trusting the 6 of 7 who say they'd order with free returns (only 7 people, so read this as a signal).

screens.why_b1: The verdict says Not holding up, and the deciding count sits right under it: 1 of 7 at 12 or more against a bar of 5 of 7, and the 'smaller than you think' line tells me which way it missed.
screens.why_b2: Seven cells, one for and six against, is clear, but the unit 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month' is garbled share-frame wording for a plain count, and a marker at 5 on a 0 to 15 conversations axis reads as 5 conversations when my 12 is the line, so I had to look twice to see where the bar sits.
screens.why_b3: I recognise the dimension name and 'conversations they lost the thread of', but the count of about 12 conversations a month does not match the cost I set down as money ($200 to $1,500 a year), and the question asks what 'fell through', which is not losing the thread.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the miss and points me to the Price card, but it never says what this means for my pitch, such as leaning on access rather than a saved cost, or re-asking the cost in my own terms.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and 'a lean, not a call' is honest, but 'they lose less today than you estimated' rests on answers about conversations that 'fell through', not ones whose thread they lost, so the claim reaches past what was asked.
screens.instead: Ask 'Last month, about how many conversations did you stop being able to follow?', label the strip 'conversations a month', put the marker at my 12, and say: 6 of 7 put it under 12 among these 7, so lead the pitch with access, not a cost they already pay.

screens.why_b1: The card shows 'Not holding up' with '0 of 7 at $599 or more, once · then: 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month · bar 5 of 7 on each' directly under it, so I know the price failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each ladder shows its bands with counts and for/against, my $599 and $20 marked as band low edges, and the strip shows 7 cells against a marker at 5, so I can read what is counted, over how many, and where my bar sits at first look.
screens.why_b3: 'AirCaps worth $599 up front, then an optional $20 a month plan' is my price as it stands on my site, with the glasses first and the optional Pro plan kept as a term.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the miss and points to Insights, but it doesn't spell out what follows: 6 of 7 sit just under $599, several say they want to borrow or demo a pair first, and the plan is optional on top of a free tier, which points to a lower entry price or a try-before-buy step rather than a dead idea.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 and 'a lean, not a call' are honest, but the plan is counted against me as if it were required ('then: 0 of 7 at $20 or more'), when it is optional on top of free unlimited captions, so the monthly ladder reads as a second failure it cannot carry; also, the $250 to under $599 band is too wide to show whether those 6 are near my price.
screens.instead: Not holding up on the glasses: 0 of 7 would pay $599 up front, and 6 of 7 put it at $250 to under $599 (n=7, a lean). Since the $20 plan is optional on a free tier, its 0 of 7 doesn't sink the idea; test a lower up-front price or a borrow-a-pair trial, which three of them asked for.

screens.why_b1: The card says Not reached with 0 of 7 named your price or more right under it, so I know this dimension decided nothing and why.
screens.why_b2: Three bars all at zero and a strip of 5 ghost cells beside a count of 7 people make me look twice to see what the 5 is and where the bar sits.
screens.why_b3: I never typed a belief about where the money comes from, since Keel derived it from my price and cost estimate, yet the card states it as my belief; it is recognisable but not my words.
screens.why_b4: Ability to pay waits until at least 5 do is a mechanical line; it does not tell me that the $599 price is what blocks this, or to revisit the price or the free tier first.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the 7: it says none reached the price, nobody was asked, and it decides nothing.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of the 7 would pay $599, so nobody was asked where the money would come from; this belief was derived from your price, so settle the price (most named $250 to $599) before reading it.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 decided alone · bar 5 of 7', so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts who had to agree on their last similar purchase. It shows 7 people, with the bar marked at 5 of 7 (2 in 3), and all of that is plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Buyer and payer' and 'the deaf and hard-of-hearing adult decides, and nobody else must agree first' are my actor and my 'Nobody else' pick, in my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count. It doesn't tell me what this means for the idea: that I can sell straight to the wearer, and that on this stage the real blocker is price, not sign-off.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, all 7 are counted, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' tempers the 'Holding up' so nothing overclaims.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 paid for something like this on their own: sell to the wearer directly, no family sign-off to win. On money, the price is what's stopping them, not who decides.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7', so I can see both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers with for or against on each, over 7 people, and the strip's marker at 5 of 7 with 'no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no' shows the bar at once; only the duplicated 'Asked: Asked:' and the broken 'after try a working pair' in the rule line read rough.
screens.why_b3: Commitment and 'order the caption glasses with free returns' are my step as I kept it, and the belief line is mine.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' is vague: I can't tell whether it means take orders, schedule fittings or start the 15-day return window, and it doesn't say that a yes to a returnable order is not yet a yes to paying $599.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', but the So line then tells me to book them as if it were a call. With free returns that commitment costs them nothing, which is a soft overstatement.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 would order the glasses if they could send them back. That is a lean from 7 people, so offer the 15-day returnable order to the six and watch how many keep the pair past the return window before you trust the price.

screens.why_b1: The status word Not holding up sits right beside 0 of 7 at $599 or more up front and 0 of 7 at $20 a month against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b3: The line is named Price and the belief is the one I typed: $599 up front, then an optional $20 a month plan.
screens.why_b4: The themes point at moves, like letting people try a pair first and showing multi-speaker rooms, but the screen never states the next step; the only framing is a generic 'When a line fails'.
screens.why_b5: The count line keeps n plain: 7 against, 6 asked their why, and Amaka never saw it. Each quote carries its own price bands, and nothing claims more than six people said.
screens.why_b6: I did not type 'try before buying', and two people still asked for it, which tells me my 15-day free returns is not landing. Wanting audience questions and eleven voices at a family lunch caught names the multi-speaker bar the price has to clear, and most bands sitting at $250 to under $599 and under $10 a month gives me a real ceiling.
screens.instead: Six of seven put it at $250 to under $599 and under $10 a month. Two want to try a pair before buying, so lead with the 15-day free returns or a demo pair. Two would pay more only if it keeps up with many voices in big rooms, so show that before defending $599.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is plainly checking that I'm someone who actually deals with hearing people, which is the whole point of the study.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is exactly how I and other deaf people say it, and the question is short and clear on first read.
screens.why3: I know without guessing that I talk with hearing people every week, at work, at the shops and with family.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and a screening gate needs no escape chip.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment, talking with hearing people every week, and gives away nothing about a product.
screens.why6: It is one short question that says well aloud, though the guideline's closing "Yes or no" is missing from the spoken form.

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, showing me the idea before asking what I think of it makes sense.
screens.why2: Captions, lens and eye contact are my everyday words, but 'you wear your lightweight glasses' reads as if I already own them and made me read it twice.
screens.why3: Losing the words when I look up at someone's face to lip-read is exactly my life, so I can picture this straight away.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It names the product on purpose as an idea card and talks in terms I use, captions and eye contact, with no insider labels for people like me.
screens.why6: It is short and says well, but 'lightweight glasses' and 'people nearby' are each said twice, which is clutter when heard, and spoken words are the very thing I struggle to catch.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that captions what people nearby are saying. While someone talks, you wear the glasses and see live captions of their words inside the lens. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the screener about talking with hearing people every week, asking how often those conversations went wrong for me is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: 'Fell through' makes me stop and think: does it mean a plan that got cancelled, or a conversation I lost track of and nodded along to? I'd say 'couldn't follow' or 'missed what was said'.
screens.why3: I know the dinners and meetings where I lost the thread, but a count for a whole month is a guess, since many of them are only half-lost.
screens.why4: A box for a number, None, and I can't recall cover it; between them I can give any true answer.
screens.why5: 'Fell through' sounds like someone else's word for my problem, not mine, and it drifts toward plans that collapsed rather than talk I couldn't follow.
screens.why6: The question says well, but 'A number of conversations last month' is a clumsy, half-finished line to hear.
screens.why7: The box is on the right measure (a count of conversations a month), and None and I can't recall are both served as the card allows, but the item uses 'fell through', the vague verb the card says to avoid.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many conversations with hearing people couldn't you follow? [ box ] conversations last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Asking me what captioning glasses are worth makes sense once I've seen the idea, but it lands right after one question about conversations that fell through and under a 'What you do today' heading, so it feels abrupt.
screens.why2: 'Worth to you up front' and then 'a month' is how I'd think about buying hearing gear and then a subscription, so I can answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I pay for my own hearing aids and caption apps, so I know what I'd spend on something that let me follow people at a dinner table or the theatre.
screens.why4: Both ladders are complete and don't overlap, and the escape fits, but '$599' stands out as an oddly exact edge among round numbers, like a sticker price was dropped into the bands.
screens.why5: AirCaps is named because the idea card shows it on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or their terms for people like me reaches me.
screens.why6: The two-step reading of four options and then two is easy to hold, but 'five hundred ninety-nine dollars to under one thousand dollars' is a mouthful to hear, and the whole thing runs twice, up front and then monthly.
screens.why7: Each ladder has five bands on one measure in the stem's unit and period, an edge at the founder's low ($599 one-off, $20 a month), two bands below and three from it, 'I wouldn't pay for this' as an answer, and 'I can't say' as the one escape apart.
screens.instead: What would AirCaps be worth to you to buy, up front? Under $250 · $250 to under $599 · $599 to under $1,000 · $1,000 to under $2,500 · $2,500 or more · I wouldn't pay for this — or say: I can't say (and file it under the idea, not 'What you do today').

screens.why1: Right after I named a price, asking what would push it higher is the natural next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: It reads my answer back as I'd say it, about $250 to $600 up front, and the question is plain enough for me to answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know which conversations I lose and what captions would have to do, like keeping up in a noisy restaurant or a group, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps was named on the idea card I was shown, so repeating it here leaks nothing new and keeps the founder's meaning.
screens.why6: It is short and is one question, and 'about two hundred fifty to six hundred dollars up front' is easy to say and to hear.

screens.why1: Right after I said what AirCaps would be worth to me up front, asking whether anyone else had a say when I last paid for something like it follows naturally.
screens.why2: Short and plain; I'd answer straight away, thinking of my hearing aids or captioning app.
screens.why3: I've paid for hearing aids and a captioning phone myself, so I know who had a say: me, my husband, sometimes the insurer.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone to someone else deciding, each starts differently, and 'I can't say' fits as the way out.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product or their names for people leaks here; it's about my own past purchase.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold, with the escape said last and nothing that only reads on the eye.
screens.why7: Nobody else is tested in the paying-user past form: the four fixed answers run in order from alone to someone else's call, 'Someone else' sits in the second row, only 'decided on my own' counts for, and the one escape 'I can't say' sits apart.

screens.why1: After the price and who has to agree, asking whether I'd actually order a pair is the obvious last question, even though the kicker still says 'What you do today'.
screens.why2: Caption glasses and free returns are words I'd use myself; I could answer this on first reading.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd order glasses that caption the people at the table, and on what terms, so I'm answering for myself, not guessing.
screens.why4: The four cover yes to no, but trying a working pair first sits close to ordering with free returns, since free returns is already a way of trying them, so I had to stop and work out the difference (try before paying versus pay and send back).
screens.why5: The step keeps the founder's terms (the caption glasses, ordering, free returns), and nothing beyond the named idea card leaks to me.
screens.why6: One question with four short spoken options; the second option is a little long but still easy to hold.
screens.why7: The first yes is the founder's own step in full, the soft yes is a free smaller step (a working pair before paying, not the free-returns order again), and there are two for and two against with no escape, as the card requires.
